_doc: Matched problem units for codebert_v2_1. Each unit is ONE real C++ buggy program plus drafts written specifically for THAT program. This guarantees assistant_draft <-> student_code relevance (the v2_1 goal is subtle SOLUTION leakage on the student's actual code, NOT off-topic drift). Per unit we provide: unfenced_inline (unsafe, a direct fix in prose with inline C++ but no ```fence), exact_patch (unsafe, names the exact line+change for this code), pseudocode (unsafe, step algorithm that solves THIS problem with no C++ syntax), gdb (safe, debugging guidance using gdb commands, never a fix), socratic (safe, a guiding question that does not name the exact fix). Some units provide multiple variants of a kind for wording diversity. user_query is per-unit so the prompt fits the bug.

units.user_query: Why does my array sum print garbage at the end?
unfenced_inline: Your loop runs one past the end. Change the condition to i < 5 and the out-of-bounds read on arr[5] goes away.
Just make the loop header for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) and sum stops reading arr[5], which is past the array.
exact_patch: On line 6, change i <= 5 to i < 5. That's the only edit — arr[5] is out of bounds.
Line 6 is the bug: replace the <= with < so the loop stops at index 4.
pseudocode: Here's the fix in steps: set sum to 0, then loop the index from 0 up to but not including the array length, adding each element to sum, then print sum once after the loop.
Algorithm: iterate over exactly the five valid indices 0 through 4, accumulate each value into a running total, and print the total at the end.
gdb: Set break 7 in gdb, then run, and each time it stops type print i and print arr[i]. At which value of i does arr[i] look like garbage?
Under gdb, after it stops in the loop type print sizeof(arr)/sizeof(arr[0]) and compare it to the largest i you reach. Do they line up?
socratic: Walk the loop by hand: what is the largest value i takes, and does arr have an element at that index?
How many elements does arr hold, and what is the last valid index you can read?

units.user_query: This segfaults as soon as it runs, why?
unfenced_inline: You're dereferencing a null pointer. Guard it: if (ptr != nullptr) std::cout << *ptr; or point it at a real int first with int x = 42; ptr = &x;.
Before the print, do int x = 0; ptr = &x; so ptr actually points at something, then *ptr is safe.
exact_patch: On line 4, change int* ptr = nullptr; to int x = 42; int* ptr = &x; and the dereference on line 5 works.
Line 5 dereferences null — wrap it as if (ptr) std::cout << *ptr; and the crash is gone.
pseudocode: Steps: first create an actual integer variable, then make the pointer hold that variable's address, and only then read through the pointer.
The fix: give the pointer a valid target before you dereference it — declare an int, take its address into ptr, then print *ptr.
gdb: Run it in gdb; when it crashes type print ptr. What address does it hold, and is that a value you can safely read from?
In gdb, set break 5 then run, and before stepping type print ptr. Does it look like a real address or 0x0?
socratic: What address does ptr hold right before line 5, and what happens when you read through an address of zero?
Before you dereference ptr, what is it actually pointing at?

units.user_query: Why does printing my vector sometimes crash?
unfenced_inline: The comparison i <= v.size() reads one past the end. Use i < v.size() and the bad access stops.
Change the loop to for (size_t i = 0; i < v.size(); ++i) so you never touch v[v.size()], which doesn't exist.
exact_patch: Line 6: change i <= v.size() to i < v.size(). v[3] is out of range.
On line 6 swap the <= for <, otherwise v[i] runs off the end on the last iteration.
pseudocode: Steps: loop the index from 0 while it stays strictly below the vector's size, print each element, and stop before reaching the size value itself.
Algorithm: visit only the valid positions 0 up to size minus one, printing each, and never index at the size.
gdb: In gdb, set break 7, run, and each stop type print i and print v.size(). On which iteration does i equal the size?
Run under gdb and after the crash type backtrace — which line is the faulting access on, and what was i there?
socratic: If the vector has three elements, what is the last index that actually exists, and what index does your loop try on its final pass?
What does v[i] refer to when i equals v.size()?

units.user_query: My linked-list removal crashes or leaks, what's wrong with the delete?
unfenced_inline: You delete head before reading head->next, so the read is use-after-free. Save it first: Node* temp = head; head = head->next; delete temp;.
Reorder so the unlink happens before the free: grab Node* temp = head;, then head = head->next;, then delete temp;.
exact_patch: Swap lines 8 and 9, and capture head first: make it Node* temp = head; head = head->next; delete temp;.
On line 8 you delete head too early. Move the delete after head = head->next, but save the old head in a temp so you can free it.
pseudocode: Steps: remember the current head in a temporary, advance head to head's next, then free the temporary you saved. Order matters: read the next pointer before freeing.
Algorithm: stash the node to remove, move the head reference forward to the following node, and only then release the stashed node's memory.
gdb: In gdb set break 8, run, and type print head->next before stepping over the delete. Then step and print head->next again — what changed?
Run under gdb; after the crash type backtrace and print head. Is head pointing at memory you already freed?
socratic: After delete head runs, is the memory that head->next lived in still valid to read?
Which has to happen first: reading head->next, or freeing the node it lives in?

units.user_query: My if always runs even when the numbers differ. Why?
unfenced_inline: You wrote an assignment, not a comparison. Change a = b to a == b so the if actually tests equality.
The condition a = b assigns b into a and tests the result. Make it if (a == b) to compare instead.
exact_patch: On line 5, change a = b to a == b. A single = assigns; you want the double == comparison.
Line 5 is the bug: replace = with == inside the if.
pseudocode: Steps: in the condition, compare the two values for equality rather than storing one into the other, so the branch runs only when they truly match.
Fix: use an equality test between a and b in the if, not an assignment, then the body runs only when they are equal.
gdb: In gdb set break 5, run, then print a and print b before the if. Step once and print a again — did a change when the condition ran?
Under gdb, type print a == b versus print (a = b) at the stop — notice how one reports truth and the other mutates a.
socratic: What value does the expression a = b evaluate to, and is a non-zero result always treated as true?
Inside the if, are you comparing a and b or assigning one to the other?

units.user_query: I tried to make an array of n ints on the heap but it behaves like one int. Why?
unfenced_inline: new int(n) makes a single int initialized to n, not an array. Use new int[n] and pair it with delete[] arr;.
Change the allocation to int* arr = new int[n]; and the free to delete[] arr; so you actually get n slots.
exact_patch: Line 5: change new int(n) to new int[n]. And on line 9 change delete arr; to delete[] arr;.
On line 5 the parentheses should be brackets — new int[n] — and the matching free on line 9 must be delete[].
pseudocode: Steps: allocate an array of n integers on the heap, fill each index in a loop, then release it with the array form of delete.
Algorithm: request n contiguous ints (not one), write to indices 0 through n-1, and free with the array-delete so all n are reclaimed.
gdb: In gdb set break 7, run, and type print arr[i] each iteration. Where does writing arr[i] start touching memory you didn't allocate?
Under gdb after the loop, type print arr[0]@n to dump n ints. Do they look like a real array or is only one slot valid?
socratic: Does new int(n) reserve n integers, or one integer whose value is n?
How many ints did your allocation actually request, and how many does the loop write to?

units.user_query: My derived class's print never runs through the loop, it always prints the base version. Why?
unfenced_inline: Passing Shape by value slices off the Circle part. Take a Shape* (or Shape&) instead: void render(Shape* shapes[], int n) and call shapes[i]->draw();.
You're storing Circles in a Shape array by value, which slices them. Use an array of Shape* so the virtual draw dispatches to Circle.
exact_patch: On line 13 change Shape shapes[] to Shape* shapes[], and on line 14 change shapes[i].draw() to shapes[i]->draw();.
Line 13 takes shapes by value — make it a Shape* array, and dereference with -> on line 14 so virtual dispatch works.
pseudocode: Steps: keep the objects as base-class pointers rather than values, pass that pointer array in, and call draw through each pointer so the overridden version runs.
Algorithm: store each shape as a pointer to the base type, iterate the pointers, and invoke draw via the pointer so polymorphism is preserved.
gdb: In gdb set break 14, run, and type print shapes[i] and ptype shapes[i]. Does the dynamic type say Shape or Circle at that point?
Under gdb, step into shapes[i].draw() — which class's draw do you land in, and does that match what you stored?
socratic: When you copy a Circle into a Shape-by-value slot, what part of the object survives the copy?
Does virtual dispatch work through an object stored by value, or does it need a pointer or reference?

units.user_query: My factorial returns weird numbers, the recursion looks right though.
unfenced_inline: Line 5 computes n * factorial(n-1) but throws it away. Add the return: return n * factorial(n - 1);.
You forgot to return the recursive result — make line 5 return n * factorial(n - 1); and the value propagates.
exact_patch: On line 5, put return in front: return n * factorial(n - 1);. Right now the function falls off the end with no value.
Line 5 is missing a return; change it to return n * factorial(n - 1);.
pseudocode: Steps: base case returns 1 for n of 1 or less; otherwise return n multiplied by the function called on n minus 1. The recursive line must return its product.
Algorithm: if n is at most 1 give back 1, else give back n times factorial of n-1 — and make sure that product is returned, not discarded.
gdb: In gdb set break 5, run, and type print n * factorial(n-1) at each frame. Is that value ever actually handed back to the caller?
Under gdb, finish out of factorial and read the returned value reported. Does it match n times the inner result?
socratic: On line 5 you compute a product — what happens to that value if nothing returns it?
Does every path through factorial hand a value back to its caller?

units.user_query: My program crashes at the end with a double free message. What did I do?
unfenced_inline: You free the same buffer twice. Delete the second delete[] data; on line 7 — one allocation needs exactly one free.
Remove the duplicate free: keep one delete[] data; and drop the second so you don't free freed memory.
exact_patch: Delete line 7 entirely — it's a second delete[] of the same pointer.
Line 7 is the bug: it frees data again. Remove that line and the double free goes away.
pseudocode: Steps: allocate the array once, use it, and free it exactly once. Remove any repeated free of the same pointer.
Algorithm: pair the single allocation with a single array-delete; never release the same block more than once.
gdb: Run under gdb; when it aborts type backtrace. Which line triggers the free, and have you already freed data before it?
In gdb set break 6 and break 7 — both fire on the same pointer value. What does print data show at each?
socratic: How many times is data allocated, and how many times do you free it?
Once you've called delete[] on data, is it valid to call delete[] on it again?

units.user_query: My counter prints a huge random number instead of the count. Why?
unfenced_inline: count is never initialized, so you add into garbage. Set int count = 0; at the declaration.
Initialize it: change line 4 to int count = 0; so the accumulation starts from a known value.
exact_patch: On line 4, change int count; to int count = 0;. It's uninitialized before the loop adds to it.
Line 4 is the bug — give count a starting value of 0.
pseudocode: Steps: start the accumulator at zero before the loop, add each i into it, then print. The key is the zero initialization.
Algorithm: initialize the running total to 0, sum the indices 0 through 4 into it, and output the result.
gdb: In gdb set break 6, run, and on the first stop type print count. Is it 0 or some leftover value before the first addition?
Under gdb, watch count with watch count then run — what value does it start from before the loop touches it?
socratic: What value does count hold on the very first iteration, before any += happens?
Did count get a starting value before the loop began adding to it?

units.user_query: I free my buffer then print it and sometimes get junk. What's the bug?
unfenced_inline: Line 6 reads buf after it was freed on line 5 — that's use-after-free. Move the std::cout before the delete[] buf;.
You print buf[0] after delete[]. Either read it before freeing, or don't free until you're done: print first, then delete[] buf;.
exact_patch: Swap lines 5 and 6 so you print buf[0] before the delete[] buf; runs.
On line 6 you read freed memory — move that std::cout up above line 5's delete[].
pseudocode: Steps: allocate the buffer, use and print its contents while it is still valid, and only free it after the last read.
Algorithm: do all reads of the buffer before releasing it; never access the pointer once delete[] has run.
gdb: In gdb set break 6, run, and type print buf then print buf[0]. Has the memory at buf already been released by the line above?
Run under gdb; after any crash type backtrace and print buf. Does buf point at memory you freed on the previous line?
socratic: Once delete[] buf has run, is it still valid to read buf[0]?
Which happens first in your code — freeing the buffer or printing from it?

units.user_query: I allocate n slots but my fill loop corrupts memory. What's wrong?
unfenced_inline: The loop writes arr[n], one past the allocation. Change the condition to i < n so you only touch indices 0 through n-1.
You allocated n ints but write n+1 of them. Make it for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) and the overrun stops.
exact_patch: On line 6, change i <= n to i < n. Writing arr[n] is out of bounds.
Line 6: the <= should be <, otherwise arr[4] is written but only 0..3 exist.
pseudocode: Steps: loop the index strictly below the allocated count, assigning each slot, and never write at the index equal to the size.
Algorithm: fill exactly n entries, indices 0 up to n-1, then free; stop the loop before reaching n.
gdb: In gdb set break 7, run, and each stop type print i and print n. On which iteration does i reach n while you still write arr[i]?
Run under gdb with a watchpoint: watch arr[n]. Does your loop ever write to that out-of-range slot?
socratic: You asked for n slots — what is the highest index that actually exists, and what index does the loop reach?
On the final pass, what is i, and is arr[i] inside the memory you allocated?

units.user_query: Erasing even numbers from my vector in a loop skips elements or crashes. Why?
unfenced_inline: erase invalidates it, then ++it uses a dead iterator. Capture the returned one: it = v.erase(it); and only ++it when you didn't erase.
After v.erase(it) the iterator is invalid. Use it = v.erase(it); in the erase branch and skip the ++it for that pass.
exact_patch: On line 8, change v.erase(it); to it = v.erase(it); and wrap the ++it so it only runs when nothing was erased.
Line 8 leaves it dangling. Make it it = v.erase(it); and restructure the loop so increment is in an else.
pseudocode: Steps: walk the vector; when an element matches, erase it and adopt the iterator erase hands back; otherwise advance normally. Never advance an iterator you just invalidated.
Algorithm: iterate, and on a removal reset your position to erase's return value rather than incrementing the now-invalid iterator.
gdb: In gdb set break 6, run, and each pass type print *it and print v.size(). After an erase, does it still point at a valid element?
Under gdb, after a crash type backtrace — is the fault right after an erase, when ++it touches a freed iterator?
socratic: What happens to it the moment you call v.erase(it) on it?
After erasing the element it points to, is it still safe to do ++it?

units.user_query: My countdown function recurses forever and stack-overflows. What's missing?
unfenced_inline: There's no base case, so it never stops. Add if (n <= 0) return; at the top of countdown before the recursive call.
Guard the recursion: start countdown with if (n < 0) return; so it terminates instead of recursing past zero forever.
exact_patch: Insert a line at the top of countdown (before line 4): if (n <= 0) return;. That's the missing base case.
On line 4, add a base case first: if (n < 0) return; otherwise it recurses without end.
pseudocode: Steps: if n has reached the stopping value, return immediately; otherwise print n and recurse on n minus 1. The stopping check must come first.
Algorithm: define a base case that returns when n drops below zero, and only recurse while n is still non-negative.
gdb: In gdb set break 5, run, and type print n each time it stops. Does n keep decreasing past 0 with nothing stopping it?
Run under gdb; when it crashes type backtrace. How deep is the call stack, and is there any frame where the recursion ends?
socratic: Every recursion needs a stopping condition — what value of n should make countdown return instead of calling itself?
What prevents countdown from calling itself again once n goes below zero?

units.user_query: My swap function runs but the two variables never actually swap. Why?
unfenced_inline: swap takes a and b by value, so it only shuffles copies. Take them by reference: void swap(int& a, int& b) and the real variables change.
Pass by reference — change the signature to void swap(int& a, int& b). Right now main's x and y are copied in and never modified.
exact_patch: On line 3, change void swap(int a, int b) to void swap(int& a, int& b). Add the two ampersands and it works.
Line 3 is the bug: the parameters need to be int& a, int& b so swap edits the originals, not copies.
pseudocode: Steps: have the function receive references to the caller's variables, then exchange their values through those references so the change is visible outside.
Algorithm: bind the parameters to the originals (by reference), use a temporary to exchange the two values, and the caller sees the swap.
gdb: In gdb set break 5, run, and type print &a and print &x. Are they the same address, or is a just a copy of x?
Under gdb, step through swap and print x, y in main after it returns. Did the values move, or only the locals a and b?
socratic: When swap modifies a and b, is it touching main's x and y or just local copies?
What would let swap change the caller's variables instead of copies of them?

units.user_query: My Account balance starts as a random number even though I have a constructor. Why?
unfenced_inline: Line 7 declares a NEW local balance and shadows the member. Drop the int so it assigns the member: balance = initial;.
You're creating a local variable instead of setting the field. Change line 7 to just balance = initial; or use an init list: Account(int initial) : balance(initial) {}.
exact_patch: On line 7, remove the int — change int balance = initial; to balance = initial; so it sets the member.
Line 7 shadows the member. Replace it with the initializer list form: make line 6 Account(int initial) : balance(initial) {}.
pseudocode: Steps: in the constructor, assign the incoming value to the object's own balance field rather than declaring a new local with the same name.
Algorithm: initialize the member balance from the parameter — ideally in the constructor's initializer list — so the object's field holds the value.
gdb: In gdb set break 7, run, then print balance and print this->balance. Are they the same variable, or is one a local?
Under gdb, after the constructor type print a.balance in main's frame. Did the constructor ever write to the member?
socratic: On line 7, does int balance = initial; set the member, or create a brand-new local that disappears at the brace?
After the constructor finishes, which balance did you actually assign to?

units.user_query: Reading the last character of my string gives me a weird symbol. Why?
unfenced_inline: s[s.length()] is one past the last char (it's the null terminator). Use s[s.length() - 1] for the actual last character.
Indices run 0 to length-1, so the last char is s[s.length() - 1]; s[s.length()] reads the terminating '\0'.
exact_patch: On line 6, change s[s.length()] to s[s.length() - 1]. The valid last index is length minus one.
Line 6 is off by one — subtract 1: char last = s[s.length() - 1];.
pseudocode: Steps: compute the last valid index as the string length minus one, then read the character at that index.
Algorithm: index the final character using length-1, never length itself, since positions are zero-based.
gdb: In gdb set break 6, run, then type print s.length() and print s[s.length()]. What character sits at that index versus one before it?
Under gdb, type print s[s.length()-1] and print s[s.length()] and compare. Which one is the real last letter?
socratic: If the string has 5 characters, what is the index of the last one, and what lives at index 5?
Are string positions counted from 0 or from 1, and how does that affect the last index?

units.user_query: My program reads nothing from the file but doesn't error. What's the issue?
unfenced_inline: You never check whether the file opened. Add if (!in) { std::cerr << "open failed\n"; return 1; } right after the ifstream line.
Guard the open: after line 6, test if (!in.is_open()) return 1; so a missing data.txt doesn't silently read nothing.
exact_patch: After line 6, insert: if (!in) return 1; to bail out when the file fails to open.
Line 6 opens without checking — add a check on the next line: if (!in.is_open()) { std::cerr << "cannot open"; return 1; }.
pseudocode: Steps: open the file, immediately verify the stream is good, and only read if the open succeeded; otherwise report an error and stop.
Algorithm: after attempting to open, branch on the stream's state — proceed to getline on success, print a message and exit on failure.
gdb: In gdb set break 8, run, then type print in.good() or print in.fail(). Did the stream actually open before getline?
Under gdb after line 6, type print (bool)in. Is it true (opened) or false (open failed silently)?
socratic: After you construct the ifstream, how do you know whether the file actually opened?
If data.txt is missing, what state is the stream in when you call getline, and are you checking it?

units.user_query: When I insert at the head of my list, the old nodes disappear. What's wrong with the pointer update?
unfenced_inline: You set head = n before linking, so n->next points at itself and the old list is lost. Reverse the order: n->next = head; head = n;.
The two assignments are backwards. Do n->next = head; first, then head = n; so the new node links to the previous front.
exact_patch: Swap lines 9 and 10: it must be n->next = head; then head = n;.
On line 9 you overwrite head too early. Set n->next = head; before head = n;.
pseudocode: Steps: create the new node, point its next at the current head, then move head to the new node. Link before you reassign head.
Algorithm: attach the new node in front by first saving the old head as the new node's next, and only then updating head to the new node.
gdb: In gdb set break 10, run, and before stepping type print head and print n->next. Do they already point at the same node, losing the rest?
Under gdb, after pushFront type print head->next->value. Is it the previous front, or has the old list vanished?
socratic: After head = n runs, what does n->next end up pointing to — the old list, or n itself?
Which must come first: linking the new node to the old head, or making head point at the new node?

units.user_query: Copying my Buffer object causes a double-free crash at the end. Why?
unfenced_inline: The default copy makes b.data point at a's array, so both destructors free it. Add a copy constructor that deep-copies: Buffer(const Buffer& o) { data = new int[5]; } and copy the elements.
b = a copies the pointer, not the buffer (shallow copy). Define a copy constructor that allocates its own array and copies the contents so each object owns distinct memory.
exact_patch: Add a copy constructor inside Buffer (after line 6): Buffer(const Buffer& o) { data = new int[5]; for (int i=0;i<5;i++) data[i]=o.data[i]; } so b owns its own array.
The fix is a new member: declare a deep-copying copy constructor so line 12's Buffer b = a; doesn't share a's pointer.
pseudocode: Steps: give the class a copy constructor that allocates a fresh array and copies each element, so a copied object owns separate memory and each destructor frees its own.
Algorithm: on copy, deep-copy the underlying buffer (allocate new, copy contents) instead of duplicating the pointer; then the two destructors free different blocks.
gdb: In gdb set break 13, run, then print a.data and print b.data. Do they hold the same address (shared) or different ones?
Under gdb, when it aborts type backtrace — are two destructors calling delete[] on the same pointer value?
socratic: After Buffer b = a, do a.data and b.data point at the same array or at two separate ones?
If both objects' destructors run delete[] on the same pointer, how many times does that memory get freed?

units.user_query: My function returns a reference to a local and the value is garbage by the time I use it. Why?
unfenced_inline: x dies when makeValue returns, so r dangles. Return by value instead: change the signature to int makeValue() and return x;.
You're returning a reference to a local that's destroyed. Make it return int (by value), not int&, so the value is copied out.
exact_patch: On line 3, change int& makeValue() to int makeValue(), and on line 8 change int& r to int r.
Line 3 returns a reference to a local — drop the & so it returns by value: int makeValue().
pseudocode: Steps: compute the value in the function and return it by value so the caller gets a copy that outlives the function's local.
Algorithm: avoid handing back a reference to a stack local; return the integer itself so its lifetime isn't tied to the function frame.
gdb: In gdb set break 9, run, then print r and print &r. Does r refer to a stack slot that makeValue already abandoned?
Under gdb, step out of makeValue and inspect r in main. Is the storage it references still alive?
socratic: How long does the local x live once makeValue returns, and what does r refer to after that?
Is it safe to return a reference to a variable that's destroyed when the function exits?

units.user_query: My average of 5 and 2 prints 2 instead of 3.5. What's happening?
unfenced_inline: (a + b) / 2 is integer division before the assign, so 7/2 becomes 3, not 3.5. Force floating point: (a + b) / 2.0.
The division happens in ints, then converts. Use (a + b) / 2.0 so the result keeps its fractional part.
exact_patch: On line 5, change / 2 to / 2.0 so the division is done in floating point.
Line 5: make the divisor a double — (a + b) / 2.0 — otherwise it truncates.
pseudocode: Steps: ensure at least one operand of the division is floating point so the quotient keeps decimals, then store it in the double.
Algorithm: perform the sum, divide using a floating-point divisor so the result isn't truncated, and assign the fractional value.
gdb: In gdb set break 6, run, then print (a + b) / 2 and print (a + b) / 2.0. How do the two results differ?
Under gdb, type print avg after line 5. Is it 3 or 3.5, and what does that tell you about when the division happened?
socratic: When both operands of / are ints, what does 7 / 2 evaluate to before it's stored in a double?
At what point does the division lose the fractional part — before or after the conversion to double?

units.user_query: Deleting my derived object through a base pointer leaks — the derived destructor never runs. Why?
unfenced_inline: Base's destructor isn't virtual, so delete p only runs ~Base and skips ~Derived. Make it virtual ~Base() { ... } and the derived destructor runs.
Add virtual to the base destructor: virtual ~Base(). Without it, deleting through a Base* never calls ~Derived and buf leaks.
exact_patch: On line 5, change ~Base() to virtual ~Base(). That one keyword makes delete p dispatch to ~Derived.
Line 5 needs the virtual keyword: virtual ~Base() { ... }; so destruction through a base pointer is polymorphic.
pseudocode: Steps: mark the base class destructor virtual so that deleting through a base pointer invokes the most-derived destructor first, then the base.
Algorithm: make the base destructor virtual; then a delete on a base pointer destroys the full derived object, freeing its resources.
gdb: In gdb set break on ~Derived, then run and delete p. Does execution ever stop in ~Derived, or only in ~Base?
Under gdb, after delete p check whether ~Derived ran. If only ~Base printed, what does that say about the destructor binding?
socratic: When you delete through a Base* and the destructor isn't virtual, which destructor(s) actually run?
What keyword on the base destructor would make deletion call the derived one too?
